pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Real Dinosaurs vs Fiction (ages 5–7): tell real dinosaurs apart from creatures often confused with them — pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (sea reptiles) were NOT dinosaurs — and understand that movie/cartoon dinosaurs are not always accurate.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports 'working scientifically' (identify, classify, and use simple criteria) and the critical-thinking seed of distinguishing evidence from fiction; no KS1 statutory dino content but strong media-literacy value.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports K–2 observation/patterns and the science-practice of using defined criteria to classify; nearest content anchor is later fossil/evidence work.
• Operational details — Two distinctions: (1) DINOSAUR vs NOT-A-DINOSAUR by a simple rule kids can apply — dinosaurs were land animals whose legs go straight DOWN under the body; pterosaurs flew (wings), plesiosaurs swam (flippers, long neck in water), so they are cousins, not dinosaurs. (Also flag the sail-backed Dimetrodon as a common not-a-dinosaur.) (2) REAL vs MOVIE — films exaggerate (roaring, wrong sizes, missing feathers, humans + dinos together) so a screen dinosaur isn't always what the real animal was like. Keep the rule concrete and forgiving; the aim is 'ask: is this really a dinosaur?', not exhaustive taxonomy.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5): says a flying pterosaur or swimming plesiosaur is not a dinosaur. Tier B (~6): applies the 'legs under the body / lived on land' idea to sort one or two creatures. Tier C (~7): sorts several creatures into dinosaur / not-a-dinosaur and gives one way a movie dinosaur can be wrong.
bestPractices: Give a single child-usable rule ('a dinosaur is a land animal with legs straight underneath') rather than formal taxonomy, then apply it to clear cases.
Use the strongest confusions as teaching cases: pterosaur (flies), plesiosaur (swims), Dimetrodon (sail) — name why each is NOT a dinosaur.
Frame flyers/swimmers as 'cousins that lived at the same time' so children don't think they're being told these animals aren't real or important.
Introduce simple media literacy: compare a movie dinosaur to the best current science (feathers, size, no upright 'zombie' hands) so 'the film isn't always right'.
Keep it playful and non-punitive — near-misses are learning moments about the rule, not wrong answers to feel bad about.
keyRepresentations: A two-bin sorter: DINOSAUR vs NOT-A-DINOSAUR, with the rule shown on each drop.
Side-by-side leg posture diagram: dinosaur legs under body vs sprawling/flippered/winged.
'Movie vs real' compare pairs (feathered vs scaly, correct vs exaggerated size).
commonMisconceptions: 'Pterodactyls/pterosaurs are flying dinosaurs' — they are flying reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Plesiosaurs (and other big sea reptiles) are dinosaurs' — they are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Dimetrodon (the sail-back) is a dinosaur' — it lived before dinosaurs and is not one.
'Movie dinosaurs show exactly what they looked like' — films exaggerate size, sounds, and often omit feathers.
'If it's big, extinct, and scaly, it's a dinosaur' — being extinct or reptile-like doesn't make an animal a dinosaur.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children apply one child-usable rule to tell real dinosaurs apart from commonly confused prehistoric creatures (flying pterosaurs, swimming plesiosaurs, sail-backed Dimetrodon), and to recognise that movie/cartoon dinosaurs are not always accurate. The rule to teach: a dinosaur was a land animal whose legs went straight DOWN underneath its body; flyers and swimmers are 'cousins' that lived at the same time, not dinosaurs. A second strand builds early media literacy: compare a screen dinosaur to current science (feathers, size, sounds, and whether humans appear alongside it) to see that confident-looking pictures aren't always right, and that some details (exact sound and colour) simply aren't known from bones. Keep it playful and non-punitive — near-misses are chances to re-apply the rule.

activities.title: Dinosaur Club bouncer: sort with a clue lens
feedback: When a pterosaur is placed in NOT-A-DINOSAUR: 'Right — wings mean it flew. It's a flying reptile, a cousin that lived at the same time, not a dinosaur.'
When a plesiosaur is placed in NOT-A-DINOSAUR: 'Yes — flippers and a long neck for swimming. A sea reptile, a cousin, not a dinosaur.'

When Dimetrodon is placed in NOT-A-DINOSAUR: 'Good spot — look at its legs: they sprawl out to the sides instead of going straight down. It lived before the dinosaurs and isn't one, even though a few real dinosaurs had sails too.'

When a pterosaur is placed in DINOSAUR (near-miss): 'Close! It looks fierce, but check the clue lens — wings, so it flew. That makes it a flying-reptile cousin, not a dinosaur. Want to try the rule again?'
When T. rex/Triceratops is placed in DINOSAUR: 'Yes — see the legs going straight down under the body, and it lived on land. That's a dinosaur.'
activities.rationale: Sorting ambiguous cases with immediate, reason-giving feedback lets the misconception (pterosaur = dinosaur) surface through the child's own choice and then be corrected, which suits a rule-application target. A drag-into-bins interaction with a feature-highlighting 'clue lens' makes the deciding criterion concrete; these are suggested interaction examples, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
learnerActions: Act as a 'bouncer' at the Dinosaur Club where only real dinosaurs get in; creatures line up one at a time: T. rex, Triceratops, a leathery-winged pterosaur, a long-necked flippered plesiosaur, and a sail-backed Dimetrodon.
For each creature, decide DINOSAUR or NOT-A-DINOSAUR and place it in that bin.
Use a 'clue lens' that highlights the deciding feature — legs straight down under the body (dinosaur), or leathery wings, flippers, or legs sprawling out to the sides (not a dinosaur).
Say or tap the reason out loud, e.g. 'wings — a flying reptile, a cousin, not a dinosaur.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being scary, scaly, big, or extinct does NOT make an animal a dinosaur — there is a simple rule (land animal, legs straight underneath) that you can apply yourself to decide.

activities.title: Movie vs real: spot what the film got wrong or guessed
feedback: On spotting missing feathers: 'Good — many dinosaurs, especially smaller ones, had feathers, so when the science version of this animal has them a bare scaly film version is wrong.'
On spotting the wrong size: 'Yes — films often make them far bigger or smaller than the real animal.'
On spotting humans with dinosaurs: 'Right — people and the dinosaurs never lived at the same time, so that part is a clear mistake.'
On questioning the roar: 'Right to wonder — we have bones, not recordings, so nobody knows the exact sound; the roar is a guess, not a fact.'
On questioning skin colour: 'Yes — bones don't tell us exact colour, so the film is guessing there, even if it looks sure.'

If the child treats the film as exactly right: 'It looks real, but remember we only have bones. Which parts are the film guessing about, and which are plain wrong? Try the feathers, the size, the people, the sound, and the colour.'
activities.rationale: Comparing a familiar media depiction against current science builds early critical thinking about evidence versus artistic guess. Separating definite errors (feathers for a feathered species, size, humans coexisting) from unknown details shown as certain (sound, colour) keeps the point honest. A side-by-side compare (or a flap that reveals the science version) makes the differences tappable and concrete; this is a suggested format, not mandatory technology.
sourceClaims: Popular film depictions of dinosaurs are frequently inaccurate (exaggerated size/sounds, missing feathers, humans coexisting), so media portrayals should be checked against current science.
learnerActions: Look at an exaggerated screen/cartoon dinosaur beside a 'best-science' version of the same animal.

Point to the things the film clearly got wrong: the wrong size, humans shown living alongside the dinosaur, and — where the best-science version of this animal has feathers — a bare scaly skin that leaves those feathers out.
Then point to the things the film shows as if certain but that we can't actually know from bones — the exact loud roar and the exact skin colour.
Name one difference out loud, e.g. 'the real one may have had feathers', 'people never lived with giant dinosaurs like this one', or 'we don't actually know the sound it made.'
activities.intendedInsight: A confident-looking picture on a screen isn't always what the science says: films exaggerate size, often leave out feathers, and sometimes show people with dinosaurs who never actually lived together, while some details (exact colour, exact sound) simply aren't known from bones, so showing them as certain is a guess dressed up as fact.

activities.title: Land / air / sea cousins gallery (scaffold)
feedback: On tapping the pterosaur: 'A flying reptile — a cousin of dinosaurs, but not one.'
On tapping the dinosaur: 'Lived on land with legs straight underneath — that's a dinosaur.'
On tapping the plesiosaur: 'A sea reptile with flippers — a cousin, not a dinosaur.'
activities.rationale: A tappable labelled gallery introduces the categories and the 'cousins lived at the same time' framing clearly, which reassures children these animals are still real and important. Treat it as a scaffold: it presents categories rather than having the child test borderline cases or hunt movie errors, so pair it with the sorting and movie-comparison activities where the discrimination is actually practised.
sourceClaims: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
learnerActions: Explore a labelled scene with three cousins: a dinosaur on land, a pterosaur in the air, a plesiosaur in the sea.
Tap each creature to reveal 'dinosaur / not a dinosaur — because…' with the deciding feature named.
Open a flap that contrasts a movie dinosaur with a real one.
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs, flying reptiles, and sea reptiles are different groups that lived at the same time; flyers and swimmers are important, real cousins — not dinosaurs, and not 'fake'.

activities.title: Ask the palaeontologist (alternative)
feedback: On asking about a pterodactyl: 'Good question — it flew, so it's a flying reptile. A cousin of dinosaurs, but not one.'
On asking about the movie roar: 'We only have bones, so no one knows the real sound — the film is guessing.'
activities.rationale: A dialogue with an expert character suits the myth-busting theme and can rehearse the reasoning, but for 5–7 a hands-on sorter gives a different kind of practice at applying the rule, so this is offered as an alternative rather than the main route. Listening and responsive questioning here give practice at hearing and restating reasons, which differs from the practice sorting gives; this is a narrow affordance, not a claim that dialogue is required or superior.
sourceClaims: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
Popular film depictions of dinosaurs are frequently inaccurate (exaggerated size/sounds, missing feathers, humans coexisting), so media portrayals should be checked against current science.
learnerActions: Pose 'is this a dinosaur?' questions to a palaeontologist character — e.g. 'Is a pterodactyl a dinosaur?' or 'Is the movie right about the roar?'
Listen to the gentle correction and then restate the rule in your own words.
Try a follow-up: give the character one creature and predict what they'll say before they answer.
activities.intendedInsight: An expert uses the same simple rule you can use — flyers and swimmers are cousins, not dinosaurs — and separates known bone evidence from guesses about sound and colour.

activities.title: Quick check: which is NOT a dinosaur? (light assessment)
feedback: On correctly naming the non-dinosaur: 'Yes — and the reason matters: leathery wings, flippers, or sprawling legs instead of a land animal with legs straight underneath.'
On naming a movie error: 'Good — feathers, size, or showing people alongside dinosaurs are things films get wrong, and sounds and colour are things films guess at.'
If a reason is missing: 'You picked the right one — now tell me the clue that gave it away.'
activities.rationale: Short categorization and selected-response items can confirm whether the rule and the media-accuracy idea have landed. These response formats check understanding rather than elicit the child's own sorting reasoning, so use them after the sorting and comparison activities, not instead of them.
learnerActions: Sort a small set of creatures into dinosaur / not-a-dinosaur.
Answer 'which of these is NOT a dinosaur?' and give the reason.
Answer 'name one thing a movie might get wrong about a dinosaur.'
activities.intendedInsight: You can state that pterosaurs flew but were not dinosaurs, that plesiosaurs swam but were not dinosaurs, and name at least one way a movie dinosaur differs from the real animal.

constraints: Teach one forgiving, child-usable rule ('a dinosaur is a land animal with legs straight underneath'), not formal taxonomy; the aim is 'ask: is this really a dinosaur?', not exhaustive classification. The rule is meant for the prehistoric animals in these activities: birds are scientifically living dinosaurs, so do not present the rule as true of every animal.
Frame flyers and swimmers as real, important 'cousins that lived at the same time' so children don't think they're being told these animals aren't real.
Keep it playful and non-punitive: near-misses are moments to re-apply the rule, not wrong answers to feel bad about.
The labelled cousins gallery is a scaffold that presents categories; it does not have the child test borderline cases or hunt movie errors, so pair it with sorting and movie-comparison tasks.
Recognition and selected-response checks confirm understanding but do not elicit the child's own sorting reasoning; use them as light assessment after the constructive tasks.

Be careful about certainty: bones do not reveal exact colour or sound, so present roars/skin colour in films as guesses shown as if certain, while missing feathers (for a feathered species), wrong size, and humans shown alongside dinosaurs are genuine errors — keep the honest point that sound and colour are unknown.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both sources are marked verified:false in the original row; the claims (upright limb posture defining dinosaurs; Dimetrodon as a pre-dinosaur synapsid; common film inaccuracies including humans coexisting) are widely accepted in palaeontology education but should be confirmed against the cited museum pages before relying on specifics.

Simplification caution: 'legs straight down under the body' is a correct but simplified cue for this age group; it is a teaching heuristic rather than the full technical definition of Dinosauria (birds, for example, are feathered flying dinosaurs), and edge cases exist beyond the scope of ages 5–7.

Framed the 'movie roar/skin colour' points as unknown-from-evidence (guesses shown as certain) rather than definitively wrong, to avoid over-claiming; the original correctAnswer already supports this. Missing feathers (for a feathered species), wrong size, and humans-with-dinosaurs remain genuine errors.
The original row rated 3D as 'poor' because the distinction is rule-based; this rewrite omits that comparative modality claim as a catalog preference rather than an established pedagogical law.

probeDeeper: What made an animal a dinosaur, if flying and swimming reptiles don't count?
Name one thing a movie might get wrong about a dinosaur.
Could scientists really know the exact roar a dinosaur made? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The book is wrong: pterosaurs (flying) and plesiosaurs (swimming) lived at the same time as dinosaurs but were NOT dinosaurs — dinosaurs were a particular family of mostly land animals. And movies aren't always accurate: we don't actually know the sounds dinosaurs made or their exact skin and colour, and many had feathers — so a roaring, scaly movie dinosaur may not match the real animal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any big prehistoric reptile is a dinosaur — flying and swimming ones included.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the boundary: pterosaurs and plesiosaurs are relatives that lived alongside dinosaurs but aren't dinosaurs; dinosaurs were land animals of a specific group.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, the book is right — flying and swimming reptiles are dinosaurs too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts pterosaurs and plesiosaurs as dinosaurs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Movies show exactly what dinosaurs were really like.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate evidence from artistic guess: we have bones, not recordings or skin colour; discuss what films add or get wrong.
errorPatterns.distractor: The movie is exactly right — that's how they really looked and sounded.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the film's sounds, skin and colour as certain fact.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs were all scaly with no feathers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce feathered-dinosaur evidence; many did have feathers, especially the smaller theropods.

responseLevels.gap: Calls any prehistoric reptile a dinosaur, and treats movie depictions as exact truth.
responseLevels.full: Separates dinosaurs from other prehistoric reptiles AND recognises film depictions are partly guesswork (sound, colour, feathers), giving a concrete example.
responseLevels.partial: Knows pterosaurs/plesiosaurs weren't dinosaurs OR that movies can be inaccurate, but not both.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A picture book shows a flying reptile (a pterosaur like Pteranodon) and a long-necked sea reptile (a plesiosaur) and calls them both 'dinosaurs'. Is the book right? And in a movie, the dinosaurs roar loudly and have dry scaly skin — is that definitely how the real ones were? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who lumps all prehistoric reptiles together calls the pterosaur and plesiosaur dinosaurs; a child who treats films as fact says the movie is exactly right. Only a child who both draws the dinosaur boundary AND knows depictions involve guesswork answers both halves.
